claim: The dorsal raphe nucleus (DR) contains the greatest number of Pet1-lineage neurons among the brainstem raphe nuclei.
source: Among the brainstem raphe nuclei, the dorsal raphe nucleus (DR) contains the greatest number of Pet1-lineage neurons, a predominantly serotonergic group distributed throughout DR subdomains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a factual assertion about the anatomical distribution of Pet1-lineage neurons.

claim: Pet1-lineage neurons in the DR are predominantly serotonergic.
source: Among the brainstem raphe nuclei, the dorsal raphe nucleus (DR) contains the greatest number of Pet1-lineage neurons, a predominantly serotonergic group distributed throughout DR subdomains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of Pet1-lineage neurons.

claim: Pet1-lineage neurons are distributed throughout DR subdomains.
source: Among the brainstem raphe nuclei, the dorsal raphe nucleus (DR) contains the greatest number of Pet1-lineage neurons, a predominantly serotonergic group distributed throughout DR subdomains.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the anatomical distribution.

claim: Pet1 neurons collectively regulate diverse physiology and behavior.
source: These neurons collectively regulate diverse physiology and behavior and are often therapeutically targeted to treat affective disorders.
evidence: This is stated as a general functional characterization of Pet1 neurons.

claim: Pet1 neurons are often therapeutically targeted to treat affective disorders.
source: These neurons collectively regulate diverse physiology and behavior and are often therapeutically targeted to treat affective disorders.
evidence: This is stated as a clinical application of Pet1 neuron research.

claim: The study describes up to fourteen neuron subtypes of DR-Pet1 neurons.
source: We describe up to fourteen neuron subtypes, many showing biased cell body distributions across the DR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Many DR-Pet1 neuron subtypes show biased cell body distributions across the DR.
source: We describe up to fourteen neuron subtypes, many showing biased cell body distributions across the DR.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by histological data in Figure 3.

claim: P2ry1-Pet1 DR neurons are the most molecularly distinct subtype.
source: We further show that P2ry1-Pet1 DR neurons – the most molecularly distinct subtype – possess unique efferent projections and electrophysiological properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the clustering analysis and differential gene expression data.

claim: P2ry1-Pet1 DR neurons possess unique efferent projections.
source: We further show that P2ry1-Pet1 DR neurons – the most molecularly distinct subtype – possess unique efferent projections and electrophysiological properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by projection mapping experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: P2ry1-Pet1 DR neurons possess unique electrophysiological properties.
source: We further show that P2ry1-Pet1 DR neurons – the most molecularly distinct subtype – possess unique efferent projections and electrophysiological properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Brainstem neurons that synthesize serotonin derive from embryonic precursors that express the transcription factor PET1 upon terminal cell division.
source: Brainstem neurons that synthesize the monoamine neurotransmitter serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine, 5-HT) (Baker et al., 1991a; Baker et al., 1991b; Baker et al., 1990; Dahlstroem and Fuxe, 1964; Ishimura et al., 1988; Steinbusch, 1981; Steinbusch et al., 1978) derive from embryonic precursors that express the transcription factor PET1 (alias FEV) upon terminal cell division (Hendricks et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Hendricks et al., 1999.

claim: PET1 shapes the serotonergic identity of neurons by regulating expression of genes required for 5-HT biosynthesis, packaging in synaptic vesicles, reuptake, and metabolism.
source: PET1 shapes the serotonergic identity of neurons by regulating expression of genes required for 5-HT biosynthesis, packaging in synaptic vesicles, reuptake, and metabolism (Hendricks et al., 2003; Krueger and Deneris, 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Wyler et al., 2015; Wyler et al., 2016), though some Pet1-lineage cells in the brain have ambiguous phenotypes with respect to their ability to synthesize and release 5-HT (Alonso et al., 2013; Barrett et al., 2016; Okaty et al., 2015; Pelosi et al., 2014; Sos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some Pet1-lineage cells in the brain have ambiguous phenotypes with respect to their ability to synthesize and release 5-HT.
source: PET1 shapes the serotonergic identity of neurons by regulating expression of genes required for 5-HT biosynthesis, packaging in synaptic vesicles, reuptake, and metabolism (Hendricks et al., 2003; Krueger and Deneris, 2008; Liu et al., 2010; Wyler et al., 2015; Wyler et al., 2016), though some Pet1-lineage cells in the brain have ambiguous phenotypes with respect to their ability to synthesize and release 5-HT (Alonso et al., 2013; Barrett et al., 2016; Okaty et al., 2015; Pelosi et al., 2014; Sos et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The mature molecular identities of Pet1-lineage neurons strongly correlate with both the embryonic progenitor domain (rhombomeric domain) from which they derive and with their mature anatomy.
source: We have previously shown that the mature molecular identities of Pet1-lineage neurons strongly correlate with both the embryonic progenitor domain (rhombomeric domain) from which they derive and with their mature anatomy (Jensen et al., 2008; Okaty et al., 2015), largely consistent with (Alonso et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding from the authors' lab with citations.

claim: Even within a given Pet1 rhombomeric sublineage and anatomical subdomain, Pet1 neurons may display different molecular and cellular phenotypes.
source: However, even within a given Pet1 rhombomeric sublineage and anatomical subdomain, Pet1 neurons may display different molecular and cellular phenotypes (Niederkofler et al., 2016; Okaty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: Pet1 neurons project widely throughout the brain.
source: Pet1 neurons project widely throughout the brain and are functionally implicated in numerous life-sustaining biological processes and human pathologies.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about Pet1 neuron anatomy.

claim: Pet1 neurons are functionally implicated in numerous life-sustaining biological processes and human pathologies.
source: Pet1 neurons project widely throughout the brain and are functionally implicated in numerous life-sustaining biological processes and human pathologies.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about Pet1 neuron function.

claim: The dorsal raphe (DR) nucleus comprises the largest anatomically defined subgroup of Pet1 expressing cells in the brain.
source: The dorsal raphe (DR) nucleus comprises the largest anatomically defined subgroup of Pet1 expressing cells in the brain, and these cells are derived from embryonic progenitors in the isthmus and rhombomere 1 (Alonso et al., 2013; Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: DR Pet1 cells are derived from embryonic progenitors in the isthmus and rhombomere 1.
source: The dorsal raphe (DR) nucleus comprises the largest anatomically defined subgroup of Pet1 expressing cells in the brain, and these cells are derived from embryonic progenitors in the isthmus and rhombomere 1 (Alonso et al., 2013; Jensen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Multiple studies have demonstrated neuronal diversity within the DR, in Pet1-expressing 5-HT neurons as well as other resident cell populations.
source: Multiple studies have demonstrated neuronal diversity within the DR, in Pet1-expressing 5-HT neurons as well as other resident cell populations (Calizo et al., 2011; Challis et al., 2013; Crawford et al., 2010; Fernandez et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2019; Kirby et al., 2003; Niederkofler et al., 2016; Prouty et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019; Spaethling et al., 2014; Vasudeva and Waterhouse, 2014; Zeisel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The study profiled 2,350 single cells with a mean of 7,521 genes detected per single cell library.
source: After stringently filtering out 'suspect' single-cell libraries (e.g. libraries with high levels of non-neuronal or mitochondrial genes, outlier library complexity, or absence/low levels of Pet1 transcripts), we obtained 2,350 single cells for further analysis, with a mean of 7,521 genes detected per single cell library (mean of 57,678 UMIs per cell), and a total of 17,231 genes detected in aggregate (after filtering out genes that were expressed in fewer than ten cells).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data obtained.

claim: The study detected a mean of 57,678 UMIs per cell.
source: After stringently filtering out 'suspect' single-cell libraries (e.g. libraries with high levels of non-neuronal or mitochondrial genes, outlier library complexity, or absence/low levels of Pet1 transcripts), we obtained 2,350 single cells for further analysis, with a mean of 7,521 genes detected per single cell library (mean of 57,678 UMIs per cell), and a total of 17,231 genes detected in aggregate (after filtering out genes that were expressed in fewer than ten cells).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data obtained.

claim: A total of 17,231 genes were detected in aggregate across all cells.
source: After stringently filtering out 'suspect' single-cell libraries (e.g. libraries with high levels of non-neuronal or mitochondrial genes, outlier library complexity, or absence/low levels of Pet1 transcripts), we obtained 2,350 single cells for further analysis, with a mean of 7,521 genes detected per single cell library (mean of 57,678 UMIs per cell), and a total of 17,231 genes detected in aggregate (after filtering out genes that were expressed in fewer than ten cells).
evidence: This is a direct report of the experimental data obtained.

claim: Tph2 gene encodes for tryptophan hydroxylase 2, the rate-limiting enzyme involved in 5-HT biosynthesis in the central nervous system.
source: The Tph2 gene encodes for tryptophan hydroxylase 2, the rate-limiting enzyme involved in 5-HT biosynthesis in the central nervous system (Walther and Bader, 2003; Walther, 2003), and all but one cluster showed consistently high Tph2 transcript expression.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: All but one cluster showed consistently high Tph2 transcript expression.
source: The Tph2 gene encodes for tryptophan hydroxylase 2, the rate-limiting enzyme involved in 5-HT biosynthesis in the central nervous system (Walther and Bader, 2003; Walther, 2003), and all but one cluster showed consistently high Tph2 transcript expression.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cluster thirteen displayed a Tph2-low expression pattern.
source: In the five- and eight-cluster-number analyses (resolution = 0.1 and 0.3, respectively), one cluster displayed a strikingly bi-modal distribution of Tph2 transcript expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,D, clusters four and six, respectively), however increasing the resolution further divided this group into a Tph2-low group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and Figure 1B, clusters eight and thirteen, respectively, corresponding to resolutions of 0.7 and 0.9) and a Tph2- 'variable' group, displaying a broader distribution of single-cell expression than other clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and Figure 1B, clusters ten and fourteen, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cluster fourteen displayed a Tph2-variable expression pattern.
source: In the five- and eight-cluster-number analyses (resolution = 0.1 and 0.3, respectively), one cluster displayed a strikingly bi-modal distribution of Tph2 transcript expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,D, clusters four and six, respectively), however increasing the resolution further divided this group into a Tph2-low group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and Figure 1B, clusters eight and thirteen, respectively, corresponding to resolutions of 0.7 and 0.9) and a Tph2- 'variable' group, displaying a broader distribution of single-cell expression than other clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G and Figure 1B, clusters ten and fourteen, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Cluster thirteen and fourteen displayed lower and more variable expression of several 5-HT neuron marker genes.
source: Beyond Tph2 expression, cluster thirteen (and to a lesser extent cluster fourteen) displayed lower and more variable expression of several 5-HT neuron marker genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Expression of 5-HT marker genes was significantly correlated with the level of Pet1 expression in cluster thirteen and fourteen cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that expression of these genes was significantly correlated with the level of Pet1 expression in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), consistent with demonstrated transcriptional regulation of 5-HT terminal identity markers by PET1 (Hendricks et al., 2003; Krueger and Deneris, 2008; Liu and Deneris, 2011; Spencer and Deneris, 2017; Wyler et al., 2015; Wyler et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Gad1 and Gad2 are paralogous genes that encode two distinct forms of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthetic enzyme glutamate decarboxylase.
source: Gad1 and Gad2 are paralogous genes that encode two distinct forms of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthetic enzyme glutamate decarboxylase (Erlander et al., 1991), and we found a sizable group of Pet1 neurons (~50%) that express high levels of Tph2 and Gad2, and to a lesser extent Gad1 (generally detected in fewer cells than Gad2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B, clusters one and two), which could be further subdivided into five sub-clusters at finer resolution (Figure 1B,C, clusters two-six).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation to Erlander et al., 1991.

claim: Approximately 50% of Pet1 neurons express high levels of Tph2 and Gad2.
source: Gad1 and Gad2 are paralogous genes that encode two distinct forms of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) synthetic enzyme glutamate decarboxylase (Erlander et al., 1991), and we found a sizable group of Pet1 neurons (~50%) that express high levels of Tph2 and Gad2, and to a lesser extent Gad1 (generally detected in fewer cells than Gad2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B, clusters one and two), which could be further subdivided into five sub-clusters at finer resolution (Figure 1B,C, clusters two-six).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Cluster six Pet1 neurons express intermediate levels of Slc17a8 transcripts.
source: One of these clusters, cluster six (Figure 1B,C), contained Pet1 neurons additionally expressing intermediate levels of transcripts for Slc17a8, encoding the vesicular glutamate transporter 3 (Fremeau et al., 2002; Gras et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Slc17a8 encodes the vesicular glutamate transporter 3.
source: One of these clusters, cluster six (Figure 1B,C), contained Pet1 neurons additionally expressing intermediate levels of transcripts for Slc17a8, encoding the vesicular glutamate transporter 3 (Fremeau et al., 2002; Gras et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Cluster six neurons had the highest expression of Gad1 relative to other groups.
source: Notably, this group of neurons also had the highest expression of Gad1 relative to other groups.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: High expression levels of Slc17a8 transcripts were detected in approximately 46% of profiled Pet1 neurons.
source: High expression levels of Slc17a8 transcripts were detected in ~46% of profiled Pet1 neurons, comprising eight clusters at finer resolution (Figure 1B,C, clusters seven to fourteen), including the Tph2-low and Tph2-variable clusters (Figure 1B,C, clusters thirteen and fourteen).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Cluster twelve is characterized by high transcript expression of Tph2, Slc17a8, and Met.
source: The most striking outlier group of Pet1 neurons (cluster twelve in Figure 1B,C) is characterized by high transcript expression of Tph2, Slc17a8, and Met, the latter encoding the MET proto-oncogene (also known as hepatocyte growth factor receptor) (Iyer et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Met encodes the MET proto-oncogene (also known as hepatocyte growth factor receptor).
source: The most striking outlier group of Pet1 neurons (cluster twelve in Figure 1B,C) is characterized by high transcript expression of Tph2, Slc17a8, and Met, the latter encoding the MET proto-oncogene (also known as hepatocyte growth factor receptor) (Iyer et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citation.

claim: Cluster twelve consistently clustered separately from all other groups at all resolutions analyzed.
source: This group of cells consistently clustered separately from all other groups at all resolutions analyzed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cluster one comprises approximately 4% of Pet1 neurons.
source: At the finest resolution of 0.9, the remaining 4% of Pet1 neurons, comprising cluster one, expressed high levels of Tph2 transcripts but only sporadically expressed transcripts for Gad2, Gad1, or Slc17a8 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Cluster one neurons expressed high levels of Tph2 transcripts but only sporadically expressed transcripts for Gad2, Gad1, or Slc17a8.
source: At the finest resolution of 0.9, the remaining 4% of Pet1 neurons, comprising cluster one, expressed high levels of Tph2 transcripts but only sporadically expressed transcripts for Gad2, Gad1, or Slc17a8 (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Met-expressing Pet1 neurons have been previously reported in mice in the caudal DR and the median raphe.
source: Met-expressing Pet1 neurons have been previously reported in mice, both at the transcript and protein levels, specifically in the caudal DR and the median raphe (MR) (Kast et al., 2017; Okaty et al., 2015; Wu and Levitt, 2013) and more recently (Huang et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to previous studies.

claim: Slc17a8- and Gad1/2-expressing DR Pet1 neurons have been previously reported in mice and rats.
source: Likewise, Slc17a8- and Gad1/2-expressing DR Pet1 neurons have been previously reported in mice and rats, as demonstrated by mRNA in situ, immunocytochemistry, and RNA-seq (Amilhon et al., 2010; Commons, 2009; Fu et al., 2010; Gagnon and Parent, 2014; Gras et al., 2002; Herzog et al., 2004; Hioki, 2004; Hioki et al., 2010; Huang et al., 2019; Okaty et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2019; Rood et al., 2014; Shikanai et al., 2012; Spaethling et al., 2014; Voisin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Depolarization-induced glutamate release by DR Pet1/5-HT neurons has been demonstrated by a number of groups.
source: Consistent with functional expression of VGLUT3 protein (encoded by the gene Slc17a8), which allows for filling of synaptic vesicles with the excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate, depolarization-induced glutamate release by DR Pet1/5-HT neurons has been demonstrated by a number of groups (Johnson, 1994; Kapoor et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2014; Sengupta et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to multiple studies.

claim: VGLUT3 is thought to interact with vesicular monoamine transporter two to enhance the loading of 5-HT into synaptic vesicles by increasing the pH gradient across vesicular membranes.
source: Additionally, VGLUT3 is thought to interact with vesicular monoamine transporter two (encoded by Slc18a2, alias Vmat2; Erickson et al., 1992) to enhance the loading of 5-HT into synaptic vesicles by increasing the pH gradient across vesicular membranes, a process referred to as 'vesicle-filling synergy' (Amilhon et al., 2010; El Mestikawy et al., 2011; Münster-Wandowski et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: GABA-release by Pet1 DR neurons has not been reported.
source: GABA-release by Pet1 DR neurons, on the other hand, has not been reported, thus the functional consequences of Gad1 and Gad2 transcript expression are presently unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: The functional consequences of Gad1 and Gad2 transcript expression in Pet1 DR neurons are presently unknown.
source: GABA-release by Pet1 DR neurons, on the other hand, has not been reported, thus the functional consequences of Gad1 and Gad2 transcript expression are presently unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Pet1 neuron subtypes defined by transcriptomic clustering show differential expression of a number of neurotransmitter-related and neuropeptide-encoding genes.
source: Pet1 neuron subtypes defined by transcriptomic clustering also show differential expression of a number of neurotransmitter-related and neuropeptide-encoding genes (Figure 2 Neurotransmitters and Neuropeptides dot plot).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Trh transcript expression is significantly enriched in cluster two Pet1 neurons.
source: Transcript expression of Trh, encoding thyrotropin-releasing hormone, is significantly enriched in cluster two Pet1 neurons and detected in clusters four and six (Figure 1D and Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figures 1D and 2.

claim: Pdyn is enriched in clusters five, six, and fourteen.
source: Pdyn, encoding the preprohormone prodynorphin is enriched in clusters five, six, and fourteen.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Prodynorphin is the precursor protein to the opioid polypeptide dynorphin.
source: Prodynorphin is the precursor protein to the opioid polypeptide dynorphin, which predominately binds the kappa-opioid receptor to produce a variety of effects, such as analgesia and dysphoria (Bruchas et al., 2010; Chavkin et al., 1982; Land et al., 2008; Land et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Nos1 expression is significantly enriched in cluster five, nine, and eleven.
source: Expression of Nos1, encoding nitric oxide synthase 1, is significantly enriched in cluster five, nine, and eleven.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The anatomical distribution of nitric oxide expressing DR 5-HT neurons in rodents has been characterized previously as being predominately midline in the DR.
source: The anatomical distribution of nitric oxide expressing DR 5-HT neurons in rodents has been characterized previously as being predominately midline in the DR (Fu et al., 2010; Prouty et al., 2017; Vasudeva et al., 2011; Vasudeva and Waterhouse, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Cluster nine shows enriched expression of Crh, encoding corticotropin-releasing hormone.
source: Cluster nine also shows enriched expression of Crh, encoding corticotropin-releasing hormone.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cluster twelve neurons show strong enrichment for Oprm1, P2ry1, Rxfp1, S1pr3, and Tacr3 transcripts.
source: For example, cluster twelve neurons show strong enrichment for opioid receptor mu (Oprm1), purine receptor y1 (P2ry1), relaxin family peptide receptor 1 (Rxfp1), sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor 3 (S1pr3), and tachykinin receptor 3 (Tacr3) transcripts.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cluster twelve neurons lack expression of transcripts for many GPCRs expressed by the majority of other Pet1 neurons, such as presynaptic 5-HT autoreceptors encoded by Htr1b and Htr1d.
source: Moreover, they lack expression of transcripts for many GPCRs expressed by the majority of other Pet1 neurons, such as presynaptic 5-HT autoreceptors, encoded by Htr1b and Htr1d, as well as orexin and histamine receptors (e.g. Hcrtr1, Hcrtr2, Hrh1, Hrh3), whose protein products are involved in the regulation of arousal.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hrh1 and Hcrtr1 transcripts were the most abundant in clusters one through four.
source: We found that histamine receptor 1 (Hrh1) and hypocretin (alias orexin) receptor 1 (Hcrtr1) transcripts were the most abundant in clusters one through four, and histamine receptor 3 (Hrh3) transcripts were the most abundant in clusters two through six.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Hcrtr2 transcripts showed a somewhat complementary expression pattern, with the highest levels in clusters seven through eleven, as well as cluster three.
source: Hypocretin receptor 2 (Hcrtr2) transcripts showed a somewhat complementary expression pattern, with the highest levels in clusters seven through eleven, as well as cluster three.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Npy2r is enriched in clusters seven and ten.
source: Other GPCR transcripts with notable expression patterns are neuropeptide Y receptor Y2 (Npy2r), enriched in clusters seven and ten, cannabinoid receptor 1 (Cnr1) and 5-HT receptor 2C (Htr2c), enriched in clusters thirteen and fourteen, and Gpr101, an 'orphan' GPCR thought to play a role in the growth hormone releasing-growth hormone signaling axis (GHRH-GH axis) (Trivellin et al., 2016; Trivellin et al., 2018), enriched in cluster fourteen.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Cnr1 and Htr2c are enriched in clusters thirteen and fourteen.
source: Other GPCR transcripts with notable expression patterns are neuropeptide Y receptor Y2 (Npy2r), enriched in clusters seven and ten, cannabinoid receptor 1 (Cnr1) and 5-HT receptor 2C (Htr2c), enriched in clusters thirteen and fourteen, and Gpr101, an 'orphan' GPCR thought to play a role in the growth hormone releasing-growth hormone signaling axis (GHRH-GH axis) (Trivellin et al., 2016; Trivellin et al., 2018), enriched in cluster fourteen.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Gpr101 is enriched in cluster fourteen.
source: Other GPCR transcripts with notable expression patterns are neuropeptide Y receptor Y2 (Npy2r), enriched in clusters seven and ten, cannabinoid receptor 1 (Cnr1) and 5-HT receptor 2C (Htr2c), enriched in clusters thirteen and fourteen, and Gpr101, an 'orphan' GPCR thought to play a role in the growth hormone releasing-growth hormone signaling axis (GHRH-GH axis) (Trivellin et al., 2016; Trivellin et al., 2018), enriched in cluster fourteen.
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Slc6a4-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons were detected throughout the full rostrocaudal and dorsoventral extent of the DR.
source: Consistent with the majority of profiled Pet1 neurons expressing high levels of Slc6a4 and Pet1 transcripts, we detected intersectional Slc6a4-cre; Pet1-Flpe fluorescently marked neurons throughout the full rostrocaudal and dorsoventral extent of the DR (Figure 3A1–A6), however the subtractive population (presumably cluster thirteen and perhaps some cluster twelve and fourteen Pet1 neurons) showed a more limited distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The subtractive population (Flpe+ but Cre-) in Slc6a4-cre; Pet1-Flpe mice showed a more limited distribution, most conspicuously concentrated in the rostromedial DR.
source: These subtractive (Flpe+ but Cre-) neurons were most conspicuously concentrated in the rostromedial DR (Figure 3A2), where only a few Slc6a4-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectional (Flpe+ and Cre+) neurons were intermingled.
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The distribution of TPH2 immunonegative Pet1 neuron cell bodies showed a very similar distribution to the subtractive neurons (Flpe-only) in Slc6a4-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-FrePe mice.
source: As another way of anatomically characterizing putative cluster thirteen Pet1 neurons, we immunostained for TPH2 in En1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-FrePe mice (the same genotype as used in some of our 10X scRNA-seq experiments), and found that the distribution of TPH2 immunonegative Pet1 neuron cell bodies showed a very similar distribution to the subtractive neurons (Flpe-only) in Slc6a4-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-FrePe mice. (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), further confirming the existence of Pet1-expressing neurons that do not express TPH2 protein (Barrett et al., 2016; Pelosi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Dual EGFP and TPH2 immunopositive cells contained significantly more Tph2 transcripts than EGFP immunopositive TPH2 immunonegative cells.
source: Across all subregions of the DR analyzed, we found that dual EGFP and TPH2 immunopositive cells contained significantly more Tph2 transcripts than EGFP immunopositive TPH2 immunonegative cells (p-value<0.01, Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests with Benjamini and Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons, see Materials and methods, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is a finding from combined immunohistology and RNAscope analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The somata of EGFP positive TPH2 negative cells were significantly smaller than dual EGFP and TPH2 positive cells.
source: Intriguingly, we also found that the somata of EGFP positive TPH2 negative cells were significantly smaller than dual EGFP and TPH2 positive cells (p-value<0.01, Wilcoxon Rank Sum tests with Benjamini and Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This is a finding from combined immunohistology and RNAscope analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Slc17a8-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons show a strong ventromedial bias in rostral portions of the DR.
source: We observed that Slc17a8-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons show a strong ventromedial bias in rostral portions of the DR (Figure 3B1–B3), and are the predominant Pet1 neuron subgroup in the more caudal midline DR (Figure 3B3–B6).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Slc17a8-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons are the predominant Pet1 neuron subgroup in the more caudal midline DR.
source: We observed that Slc17a8-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons show a strong ventromedial bias in rostral portions of the DR (Figure 3B1–B3), and are the predominant Pet1 neuron subgroup in the more caudal midline DR (Figure 3B3–B6).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The subtractive Pet1 neuron subgroup (presumably comprising Pet1 neurons from clusters one through five and partly six) show a strong dorsal and lateral bias and are largely absent from the most caudal portions of the DR.
source: By contrast, the subtractive Pet1 neuron subgroup (presumably comprising Pet1 neurons from clusters one through five and partly six) show a strong dorsal and lateral bias and are largely absent from the most caudal portions of the DR.
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was consistent overlap between intersectional recombination marked neurons and VGLUT3 protein expression, especially in medial, ventromedial, and caudal portions of the DR.
source: We found consistent overlap between intersectional recombination marked neurons and VGLUT3 protein expression, especially in medial, ventromedial, and caudal portions of the DR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–J).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistological analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–J.

claim: In the dorsal and lateral portions of the DR, a small number of Slc17a8-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons were negative for VGLUT3 antibody staining.
source: In the dorsal and lateral portions of the DR, however, where there are far fewer intersectionally labeled neurons, we observed a small number of Slc17a8-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons that were negative for VGLUT3 antibody staining, suggesting transient expression of Slc17a8 (and Slc17a8-cre) by these cells at an earlier time in their developmental history (or low Slc17a8 expression sufficient to drive Cre expression, but not VGLUT3 immunodetection).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistological analysis with interpretation.

claim: Cluster two Gad2-Trh-Tph2-Pet1 neuron cell bodies are found predominately in the dorsolateral DR, as well as the dorsomedial DR.
source: Based on manual scRNA-seq of sub-anatomically targeted Pet1 neurons, we found that cluster two Gad2-Trh-Tph2-Pet1 neuron cell bodies are found predominately in the dorsolateral DR, as well as the dorsomedial DR, whereas clusters three, four, and five appear to be more dorsomedially biased, consistent with recent reports (Huang et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from manual scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Clusters three, four, and five appear to be more dorsomedially biased.
source: Based on manual scRNA-seq of sub-anatomically targeted Pet1 neurons, we found that cluster two Gad2-Trh-Tph2-Pet1 neuron cell bodies are found predominately in the dorsolateral DR, as well as the dorsomedial DR, whereas clusters three, four, and five appear to be more dorsomedially biased, consistent with recent reports (Huang et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from manual scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cluster twelve Pet1 neurons, marked by expression of the gene Met, are the most different from all other Pet1 neurons in terms of the number of differentially expressed genes and the magnitudes of enrichment/depletion.
source: The most molecularly distinct Pet1 neuron subtype we identified, cluster twelve Met-Slc17a8-Tph2-Pet1 neurons, shows highly specific enrichment for a number of transcripts, including P2ry1, encoding purinergic receptor P2Y1, which is only sporadically expressed in other clusters (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the scRNA-seq data analysis and is also noted as consistent with other studies.

claim: P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons are largely restricted to the caudal DR where they are densely clustered dorsally, just beneath the aqueduct.
source: P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectionally marked neurons likewise show a strikingly unique anatomical distribution from the other subgroups examined, being largely restricted to the caudal DR where they are densely clustered dorsally, just beneath the aqueduct (Figure 3E5–E6).
evidence: This is a finding from histological analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The distribution of P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe intersectional neurons is consistent with previous characterizations of Met-expressing Pet1/5-HT neurons.
source: This is consistent with previous characterizations of Met-expressing Pet1/5-HT neurons (Okaty et al., 2015; Wu and Levitt, 2013), as well as other more recent characterizations (Huang et al., 2019; Kast et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as consistency with previous studies with citations.

claim: Most fibers from P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons were supra-ependymal and were found throughout the third, lateral, and fourth ventricles.
source: Strikingly, most fibers from P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons were supra-ependymal and were found throughout the third, lateral, and fourth ventricles, a property previously attributed to 5-HT neurons within the cDR (Kast et al., 2017; Mikkelsen et al., 1997; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from anatomical tracing shown in Figure 5.

claim: P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 fibers were closely apposed to proliferating cells (Ki67+) and migrating neuroblasts (doublecortin, DCX+) within the subventricular zone (SVZ) and within the rostral migratory stream (RMS).
source: Further, P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 fibers were closely apposed to proliferating cells (Ki67+) and migrating neuroblasts (doublecortin, DCX+) within the subventricular zone (SVZ) and within the rostral migratory stream (RMS) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistological analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The proximity of P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 fibers to adult neural stem cells suggests that they may constitute a serotonergic population of neurons that regulate SVZ proliferation.
source: The proximity of P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 fibers to adult neural stem cells suggests that they may constitute a serotonergic population of neurons that regulate SVZ proliferation, a process known to be regulated by 5-HT levels and that has previously been associated with the cDR (Aghajanian and Gallager, 1975; Banasr et al., 2004; Brezun and Daszuta, 1999; Hitoshi et al., 2007; Kast et al., 2017; Lorez and Richards, 1982; Mirzadeh et al., 2010; Negoias et al., 2010; Siopi et al., 2016; Soumier et al., 2010; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical proximity and cited literature on 5-HT regulation of SVZ proliferation.

claim: The predominant labeled population after retrograde AAV injection into the lateral ventricle was in the cDR, just under the aqueduct.
source: The predominant labeled population in both genotypes was in the cDR, just under the aqueduct, suggesting that P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe neurons constitute the major supraependymal projecting group of Pet1 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a finding from retrograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe neurons constitute the major supraependymal projecting group of Pet1 neurons.
source: The predominant labeled population in both genotypes was in the cDR, just under the aqueduct, suggesting that P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe neurons constitute the major supraependymal projecting group of Pet1 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an inference based on retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Some cell bodies were also found in the median raphe after retrograde AAV injection into the lateral ventricle.
source: However, in agreement with other studies that have included retrograde labeling via the lateral ventricle, some cell bodies were also found in the median raphe (Kast et al., 2017; Tong et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from retrograde tracing experiments with citation to consistent previous studies.

claim: P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons have dramatically lower excitability than the two comparison populations.
source: As demonstrated in the frequency-current (F-I) curves in Figure 6A, we found that P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons have dramatically lower excitability than the two comparison populations, requiring substantially more injected current to reach action potential threshold, and showing a roughly three-fold lower maximum firing rate.
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons showed a longer latency to first action potential.
source: Even within the regime of current injection that P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons are excitable, we found that they displayed very different spiking characteristics from other Pet1 neuron groups (Figure 6B,C), specifically showing a longer latency to first action potential (AP, Figures 6B and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: All P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons recorded showed long latency to first AP.
source: All P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons recorded (twelve neurons from three animals) showed long latency to first AP, whereas only one out of nine subtractive neurons in the P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-FL-hM3Dq cDR (from three animals) showed this phenotype and none of the Gad2-cre; Pet1-Flpe; RC-Ai65 neurons (twelve neurons from two animals).
evidence: This is a finding from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: One hundred percent of single neurons making up the Huang 5-HT V and Ren cDR subgroups map to cluster twelve Pet1 neuron subgroup.
source: For example, one hundred percent of single neurons making up the Huang 5-HT V and Ren cDR subgroups map to our cluster twelve Pet1 neuron subgroup (Met-Slc17a8-Tph2-Pet1 neurons, corresponding to neurons intersectionally captured by P2ry1-cre; Pet1-Flpe expression in the cDR shown in Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of datasets shown in Figure 7.

claim: There is high correspondence between Huang 5-HT I, Ren DR 1, and cluster two Pet1-neuron subgroup.
source: Likewise, there is high correspondence between Huang 5-HT I, Ren DR 1, and our cluster two Pet1-neuron subgroup (dorsolateral DR Gad2-Trh-Tph2-Pet1 neurons).
evidence: This is a finding from comparative analysis of datasets shown in Figure 7.

claim: The study achieved more than three-fold higher gene detection per single cell library on average than the Huang study.
source: Specifically, our study and the Ren study achieved more than three-fold higher gene detection per single cell library on average than the Huang study, thus allowing for finer-scale molecular subgroup classification.
evidence: This is a comparison of technical aspects of the different studies.

claim: The study profiled 2,350 DR Pet1 neurons, whereas Huang and Ren profiled roughly 700 and 600 DR Pet1 neurons, respectively.
source: However our higher single-cell sampling resolution – we profiled 2,350 DR Pet1 neurons, whereas Huang and Ren profiled roughly 700 and 600 DR Pet1 neurons, respectively – likely allowed us to resolve more subgroups.
evidence: This is a comparison of the number of cells profiled across studies.

claim: Identification of fourteen clusters did not occur until at least 1,700 cells were included in the analysis.
source: As expected, we found that increasing the number of cells increased the number of clusters. Identification of fourteen clusters did not occur until at least 1,700 cells were included in the analysis, and this number of clusters began to stabilize as 2,100 or more cells were included.
evidence: This is a finding from subsampling analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The number of cells sampled was more limiting than the number of UMIs in the dataset with respect to resolving fine-scale DR Pet1 neuron subgroup structure.
source: With respect to our ability to resolve fine-scale DR Pet1 neuron subgroup structure, these results indicate that while both variables are important, the number of cells sampled was more limiting than the number of UMIs in our dataset; that is, we could have uncovered a similar degree of overall cellular diversity (fourteen subtypes) with less 'complex' libraries (e.g. from more shallow sequencing), however we needed nearly 90% of the cells we sampled to consistently uncover fourteen molecular subgroups.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the subsampling analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dorsal raphe nucleus is likely one of the most extensively connected hubs in the mammalian brain.
source: The dorsal raphe nucleus is likely one of the most extensively connected hubs in the mammalian brain.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about DR connectivity.

claim: Efferent DR fibers, predominantly serotonergic (but also glutamatergic and GABAergic), collectively innervate much of the forebrain and midbrain, as well as some hindbrain nuclei.
source: Efferent DR fibers, predominantly serotonergic (but also glutamatergic and GABAergic), collectively innervate much of the forebrain and midbrain, as well as some hindbrain nuclei (Azmitia and Segal, 1978; Bang and Commons, 2012; Bang et al., 2012; Beaudet and Descarries, 1976; Fernandez et al., 2016; Gagnon and Parent, 2014; Hale and Lowry, 2011; Kast et al., 2017; Kosofsky and Molliver, 1987; Lidov et al., 1980; Lidov and Molliver, 1982; Maddaloni et al., 2017; McDevitt et al., 2014; Molliver, 1987; Muzerelle et al., 2016; O'Hearn and Molliver, 1984; Prouty et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018; Steinbusch, 1981; Steinbusch et al., 1980; Vasudeva et al., 2011; Vertes, 1991; Vertes and Kocsis, 1994), and DR afferents have been identified from as many as eighty distinct anatomical brain regions, including other brainstem raphe nuclei (Celada et al., 2001; Commons, 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2009; Levine and Jacobs, 1992; Mosko et al., 1977; Ogawa et al., 2014; Peyron et al., 1997; Peyron et al., 2018; Pollak Dorocic et al., 2014; Weissbourd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with extensive citations.

claim: DR afferents have been identified from as many as eighty distinct anatomical brain regions, including other brainstem raphe nuclei.
source: Efferent DR fibers, predominantly serotonergic (but also glutamatergic and GABAergic), collectively innervate much of the forebrain and midbrain, as well as some hindbrain nuclei (Azmitia and Segal, 1978; Bang and Commons, 2012; Bang et al., 2012; Beaudet and Descarries, 1976; Fernandez et al., 2016; Gagnon and Parent, 2014; Hale and Lowry, 2011; Kast et al., 2017; Kosofsky and Molliver, 1987; Lidov et al., 1980; Lidov and Molliver, 1982; Maddaloni et al., 2017; McDevitt et al., 2014; Molliver, 1987; Muzerelle et al., 2016; O'Hearn and Molliver, 1984; Prouty et al., 2017; Ren et al., 2018; Steinbusch, 1981; Steinbusch et al., 1980; Vasudeva et al., 2011; Vertes, 1991; Vertes and Kocsis, 1994), and DR afferents have been identified from as many as eighty distinct anatomical brain regions, including other brainstem raphe nuclei (Celada et al., 2001; Commons, 2015; Gonçalves et al., 2009; Levine and Jacobs, 1992; Mosko et al., 1977; Ogawa et al., 2014; Peyron et al., 1997; Peyron et al., 2018; Pollak Dorocic et al., 2014; Weissbourd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with extensive citations.

claim: DR neuropathology is associated with several human disorders with broad symptomatology, such as major depressive disorder, autism, and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Indeed, DR neuropathology is associated with several human disorders (or disease models thereof) with broad symptomatology, such as major depressive disorder, autism, and Alzheimer's disease (Chen et al., 2000; Dengler-Crish et al., 2017; Autism Sequencing Consortium et al., 2019; Ellegood et al., 2015; Guo and Commons, 2017; Ji et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2017; Michelsen et al., 2008; Miyazaki et al., 2005; Šimić et al., 2017; Vakalopoulos, 2017; Wang et al., 2018; Zweig et al., 1988).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.
